region.en: Alleghany Mountains and the salt-lick (traditional raiding route south)
region.zh: 阿利根尼山與鹽沼（南征傳統路線）

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. II: 'The warrior saved by pigmies'

summary.en: Falling ill on the homeward raid, a war-chief is abandoned on an Alleghany river bank. In the night three male pigmies land hurriedly and care for him, shooting two buffalo cows that rise from the neighboring salt-lick where strange animals come up out of the earth. Brought home, his story convicts the false warriors, who are punished; a large party then seeks the lick and finds it ringed with the bones of beasts the pigmies have killed.
summary.zh: 南征歸途中，一位大戰士病倒，被同袍棄於阿利根尼河岸。夜裡三位男性小人匆匆登岸照料他，並在鹽沼旁射殺自地中升起的兩頭母水牛。他歸鄉後道出實情，誣報的戰士受罰；族人往尋鹽沼，只見四野盡是小人族所殺巨獸之骨。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. The pigmies (Jogohso'') are a widespread Iroquois little-people race.

passages.text: One of a raiding party away about two years was taken quite ill on the very evening of the journey homeward; after a long consultation the party concluded to leave him, and abandoned him on the shore of one of the rivers of the Alleghany Mountains. At home the warriors were questioned about the missing war-chief and said he must have been lost or killed in the Southern country.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. II; public domain.

passages.text: During the night the sick chief lying on the bank heard the soft sounds of a canoe's approach, and saw three male pigmies landing hurriedly. Finding him, they bade him lie there until they returned, as they were going to a neighboring salt-lick where many strange animals watered, and where they were to watch for some of them to come up out of the earth. Hiding themselves, they saw a male buffalo approach and drink, and immediately two buffalo cows arose out of the lick; seeing the animals becoming restless, the pigmies wisely concluded to shoot them, and succeeded in killing the two cows.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. II; public domain.

passages.text: They returned to the man and told him they would care for him, brought him to his friends, and from his story they learned that the returned warriors were false, and they were accordingly punished. From a strong desire to see the lick, a large party searched for it and found it surrounded with bones of various large animals killed by the pigmies.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. II; public domain.

region.en: Little cave in the Seneca woods

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. II: 'The pigmy's mission'

summary.en: A pigmy living in a little cave invites a neighboring hunter, shows him the little people in great numbers with corn, huckleberries, games, bows and arrows and even war dances, then detains him until he has told the mission: 'We are to help you, and we have never injured you, but now we are going to move away from here - to where there is more danger from the giant animals, that we may help those who need our aid.'
summary.zh: 居於小洞的小人邀請鄰近的獵人入內，讓他見識成群的小人族、玉米與越橘、遊戲弓箭乃至戰舞，隨後留他聽完使命：「我們是來幫你們的，從未傷害你們；但如今我們要離開這裡——往巨獸為患之處去，幫助那些需要我們的人。」

passages.text: There was once a pigmy living in a little cave. Near him dwelt a hunter in a wigwam. The pigmy sent to him and bade him visit him. The hunter went accordingly, and saw many wonderful things; the little people themselves in great numbers, and the corn and huckleberries and other berries which they had in plenty to eat. And the pigmy said: 'This is our home, and all we have is given to us free, and although I am small I am stronger than you.' Then he showed him the games, and the bows and arrows and the dances, even the war dances, and the hunter said when he had seen it all, 'Let me go.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. II; public domain.

passages.text: But the pigmy said, 'Stay! Do you know my name? I am called Go-Ga-Ah (little fellow). I had my choice of name. I will let you out when I have told you our mission. We are to help you, and we have never injured you, but now we are going to move away from here. We are going where there is more danger from the giant animals, that we may help those who need our aid.' Then having finished his speech, he opened the door and let the hunter go on his way.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. II; public domain.

title.en: The Origin of Witches and Witch Charms: The Boy and the Snake Water
title.zh: 巫術與巫咒之起源：男孩與蛇水

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. III: 'The origin of witches and witch charms'

summary.en: A boy out hunting catches a beautiful snake and keeps it in a bark bowl of water with fibers, down and small feathers - which become living beings. Whatever he puts in the water comes alive; rubbed on his eyes, the snake-water lets him see hidden things; dipped fingers bewitch at a pointing; the draught blown from the mouth gives great light, grants night-vision, snake-shape, invisibility and swiftness; a dipped arrow or feather kills whatever it is aimed at. He then searches out the antidote roots that can undo his own bewitchments - the origin, says the tradition, of witchcraft and witch charms.
summary.zh: 男孩捕得一條美蛇，養於樹皮碗的水中，與纖維、絨毛、細羽同浸——諸物皆化為活物。凡入此水者皆得生命；抹眼可視隱物；沾指一點即令人中巫；口吹生光、夜能視物、化身為蛇、隱身疾行；蘸水之箭羽所指必死。他進而尋得可解自己所施之咒的草根——此即巫術與巫咒之起源。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Witch-practice is presented as tradition of record, not instruction.

passages.text: A certain boy while out hunting came across a beautiful snake. Taking a great fancy to it, he caught it and cared for it, feeding it on birds, and made a bark bowl in which he kept it. He put fibers, down, and small feathers into the water with the snake, and soon found that these things had become living beings. From this fact he conjectured that the snake was endowed with supernatural powers. He continued his experiments, and discovered that whatever he put into this water became alive; so he went to another swamp and got other snakes, which he put into the bowl.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

passages.text: While experimenting he saw other Indians putting things on their eyes to see sharp, so he rubbed some of this snake-water on his eyes, and climbing a tree found that he could see things even if they were hidden. He learned that by simply putting one of his fingers into the liquid and pointing it at any person that person would immediately become bewitched. By blowing the mixture from his mouth it would give a great light; by placing some in his eyes he could see in the dark and could go through all kinds of impassable places; he could become like a snake; he could even become invisible, and could travel faster than any other mortal. An arrow dipped into this liquid and shot at any living being, even if it did not hit its object, would nevertheless kill it. Having discovered the great power of this snake extract, he diligently searched for roots and herbs having the required qualities, and finally obtained antidotes which would work upon objects which he had bewitched or wounded.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

title.en: The Origin of the Great Medicine of the Senecas

region.en: Night field in the Seneca woods
region.zh: 塞內卡林中的夜間田地

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. III: 'Origin of the Seneca medicine'

summary.en: A lone hunter is wakened by singing and a drum; the field holds a hill of corn and a squash vine with three squashes. A watcher warns him he deserves to die for intruding on the sacred, but the gathered dancers pardon him and teach the secret: 'The great medicine for wounds is squash and corn.' They heat a stick and thrust it through his cheek and leg to prove how quickly the medicine heals; singing the medicine song with gourd rattles, they reveal themselves as bears, beavers and foxes flying away. The prescription - dried cob and squash pounded fine, water taken only from up the running spring - is prepared with singing at every deer's coat-change, tobacco burned as prayer.
summary.zh: 孤身獵人夜聞歌聲與鼓聲起身探看；田中有玉米之丘與三瓜之藤。守夜者斥其擅闖聖地、該死，然舞者們赦免了他，並授以秘方：「療傷之大藥，即是南瓜與玉米。」他們以燒熱的木棍穿其面頰與腿，以藥立癒為證；眾人邊搖葫蘆邊唱藥歌，最後現出原形——熊、河狸與狐——翩然而散。藥方以乾玉米心與南瓜搗細、取上游活水調製，每逢鹿換毛時唱製，焚菸草如祈禱。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. The medicine song and formula are narrated historically, not reproduced for use.

passages.text: Nearly two hundred years ago a man went into the woods on a hunting expedition, quite alone. He camped out in a field and was wakened in the night by the sound of singing and a noise like the beating of a drum. To his surprise the place had all the appearance of being inhabited: on the one hand was a hill of corn, on the other a large squash vine with three squashes on it, and three ears of corn grew apart from all the others. In the night, as he slept near by, he again heard a noise, and awakening, saw a man looking at him, who said, 'Beware! I am after you; what you saw was sacred; you deserve to die.' But the people who now gathered around said they would pardon it, and would tell him the secret they possessed: 'The great medicine for wounds,' said the man who had awakened him, 'is squash and corn; come with me and I will teach you.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

passages.text: He led him to the spot where the people were assembled, and there he saw a fire and a laurel bush which looked like iron. The crowds danced around it singing, and rattling gourd-shells. Then one of them heated a stick and thrust it right through his cheek, and then applied some of the medicine to prove how quickly it could heal the wound; then they did the same to his leg. All the time they sang the 'medicine song,' and taught it to him. Then as he turned to go home he perceived that they were not human beings as he had thought, but animals - bears, beavers, and foxes - which all flew off as he looked. They had given him directions to take one stalk of corn and dry the cob and pound it very fine, and to take one squash, cut it up and pound that; he was to take water from a running spring, always from up the stream, never down. He made up the prescription and used it with very great success, and made enough before he died to last over one hundred years.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

passages.text: This was the origin of the great medicine of the Senecas. The people sing over its preparation every time the deer changes his coat, and when it is administered to a patient they sing the medicine song, while they rattle a gourd-shell as accompaniment, and burn tobacco. Burning tobacco is the same as praying. In times of trouble or fear, after a bad dream, or any event which frightens them, they say, 'My mother went out and burned tobacco.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

title.en: A True Witch Story: The Beaver Thigh-Bone of Molly Brant's Child
title.zh: 真實巫案：莫莉布蘭特之子的河狸腿骨

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. III: 'A true witch story'

summary.en: A stingy old Seneca woman suffers great pain in her eye; the conjurer reveals she is bewitched by a poor woman she once refused milk, combing her hair over her face so he could not see her features. The witch - a Chippewa - is brought before the chief, confesses, and demands the hollow thigh-bone of a beaver from a man 'who is the child of Molly Brant, the child of Governor W. Johnson.' Spitting through the bone into scoured brass kettle water, she draws out first a spider, then a feather; the pain leaves the old woman, but the sight is not restored.
summary.zh: 塞內卡一位吝嗇老婦眼疾劇痛；占者卜出：她曾拒絕借乳給一位貧婦，因而被其行巫——那婦人以髮覆面，故他不識其貌。該巫（一名奇普瓦人）被帶至酋長前認罪，並索要「莫莉布蘭特之子、威廉莊臣總督之孫」那人的空心河狸腿骨。她經骨向擦淨的銅鍋清水吐涎，先見鍋中蜘蛛奔走，後化作羽毛；老婦痛止而目不能復明。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Named historic persons appear as lineage markers in the charm formula.

passages.text: Among the Senecas dwelt an old woman who was very stingy. All at once she began to suffer great pain in her eye. She consulted a conjurer, who went out to a bush and covered it with a tent and then began to sing, keeping time with his hand. After a while he returned to her and said: 'You are bewitched. You refused to give milk to a poor woman who came to beg of you, and she has bewitched you. I have had her house revealed to me, and I saw her, but she was combing her hair over her face, so I could not see her features.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

passages.text: Next day he tried again; then he said: 'Now I know who she is.' So they sent for a chief and told him all about it, and he brought the woman before them. She was a Chippewa and a witch. The chief had her brought to the old woman's cabin. She owned that she had bewitched her, and said, 'Fetch me the thigh-bone of a beaver from a man who is the child of Molly Brant, the child of Governor W. Johnson.' The bone was brought, and by the time it arrived she had scoured a brass kettle, and had clean water poured into it. As soon as she received the bone, which was hollow, she placed it against the eye that was not painful and spat through it. After a while she ceased spitting, and looked in the water: a spider was running around in the kettle. She covered it over with her handkerchief, then removed it, and a feather lay there instead of the spider. The pain left the old woman but the sight was not restored.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

title.en: An Incantation to Bring Rain: The Sons of Thunder in the Horizon
title.zh: 求雨之儀：地平線上的雷神諸子

region.en: Council-house of the Seneca (symbolic pin at Cattaraugus)
region.zh: 塞內卡議屋（象徵性定位於卡塔勞格斯）

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. III: 'An incantation to bring rain'

summary.en: In a dry season, with thunder-heads on the horizon, swift-footed heralds notify the people that the sons of Thunder are near and tobacco must be burned for rain. Each family offers secretly on its private altar, then bears its tithe to the council-house where the gathered tobacco is burned while the athletic dance the rain-dance. Hi-nun, pleased with the incense, calls forth huge dark banks of rain cloud and takes personal charge of the storm to wet the parched earth - for Hi-nun was considered a great lover of tobacco, but always in want of it.
summary.zh: 旱季裡，雷雲現於地平線，捷足的信使奔告眾人：雷神諸子已近，須焚菸草求雨。各家先在私壇密祭，再攜什一之菸至議屋，將聚集的菸草焚於議火之中，壯者則跳雨舞。希農樂聞菸香，召來大片烏雲，親自引導風雨潤澤焦土——人皆言希農極愛菸草，卻永遠欠缺。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Rain-rite described as custom of record.

passages.text: In a dry season, the horizon being filled with distant thunder-heads, it was customary to burn what is called by the Indians real tobacco as an offering to bring rain. On occasions of this nature the people were notified by swift-footed heralds that the children, or sons, of Thunder were in the horizon, and that tobacco must be burned in order to get some rain. Every family was supposed to have a private altar upon which its offerings were secretly made; after which said family must repair, bearing its tithe, to the council-house, where the gathered tithes of tobacco were burned in the council-fire. While the tobacco was burning, the agile and athletic danced the rain-dance.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

passages.text: When this was done, Hi-nun, pleased with the incense of the burning tobacco, called forth huge dark banks of rain clouds and took personal charge of the gathering storm to guide it to wet the dry and parched earth. Hi-nun was considered a great lover of tobacco, but always in want of it.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

title.en: Witch Transformations: The Fiery Dog, the Hog, and the White Bull
title.zh: 巫者變形：噴火之犬、豬與白牛

region.en: Buffalo Creek and Tonawanda Reservations, New York
region.zh: 紐約州水牛溪與托納萬達保留地

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. III: 'A witch in the shape of a dog'; 'A man who assumed the shape of a hog'; 'Witch transformation'

summary.en: Three witch-sighting anecdotes: on the Buffalo Reservation a man shoots a fire-streaming witch-dog and tracks the blood to the Tonawanda Reservation, where a woman lies dead of the shot; three Tonawanda boys chase a big hog to a creek bank and are told by a laughing old man that it was he himself they pursued; and a Canadian Indian follows a huge white bull with fire streaming from its nostrils until, before a house, it becomes a man with a large white blanket, ever afterward known as a witch.
summary.zh: 三則目擊巫者軼事：水牛溪保留地一男子擊中口鼻噴火的巫犬，循血跡追至托納萬達，見一婦人中彈而亡；托納萬達三少年追豬至溪畔，一位大笑的老人說他們追的正是他自己；加拿大一位印第安人追逐鼻噴火焰的巨大白牛，牛行至屋前化作披大白氈的男子——此人此後被稱為巫者。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Belief narratives of record.

passages.text: On the Buffalo Reservation a man saw a 'witch-woman' coming, with fire streaming from her mouth. Crossing a creek and obtaining his gun, the man returned and saw a dog at no great distance resting its forefeet upon a log, and it had fire streaming from its mouth and nostrils. The man fired at it and saw it fall, but as it was very dark he dared not go near it; on the following morning he went to the spot and saw where it had fallen, by the marks of blood from its wound. Tracking it by this means, he followed its path until it had reached a bridge, where the woman's tracks took the place of the dog's tracks in the path. He followed the bloody trail to the Tonawanda Reservation, where he found the woman. She had died from the effect of the shot.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

passages.text: On the Tonawanda Reservation three boys were coming down a hill when they saw a large hog, which they concluded to follow to find its home. As they pursued it they continually kicked it, and it retaliated by biting at them at times. It retreated toward the bank of a small creek, reaching which it suddenly disappeared. While searching for it they found on one of the banks an old man, who laughed and said, 'What do you seek?' They answered, 'A hog.' After some moments the old man said that it was he, himself, whom they had been chasing, and by this the boys knew that he was a witch.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

passages.text: A Canadian Indian says he saw, one evening, on the road, a white bull with fire streaming from its nostrils, which, after it had passed him, he pursued. He had never seen so large a bull, or in fact any white bull, upon the reservation. As it passed in front of a house it was transformed into a man with a large white blanket, who was ever afterward known as a witch.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

title.en: The Poison Flies and the Black-and-Yellow Bird

region.en: Deer forests of the Iroquois country

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. III: 'A superstition about flies'

summary.en: A species of fly so poisonous that the smell of them can eat the nose from a man's face nests in marked trees and often enters the horns of deer - hence a hunter's first move after shooting a deer is to examine its horns, and if they are infected to run, since the moment the animal dies the fatal insect emerges. Deer congregate around the fly-trees as if bewitched. Only the black-and-yellow woodpecker destroys them; caught with buckskin traps, its feathers fastened to the hunter's arrows make them surely bring down the deer.
summary.zh: 有一種蠅毒烈非常，僅其氣味便能蝕去人鼻。牠們在樹上築巢，蹤跡可循，常入鹿角——故獵人射鹿後必先驗角，若有感染便立即奔逃，因獸一斷氣毒蟲即破角而出。鹿群彷彿被迷住般聚於毒蠅之樹。唯有黃黑相間的啄木鳥能誅之；以鹿皮羅網捕得，其羽繫於獵人之箭，箭矢因而必中鹿身。

passages.text: There was once a species of fly so poisonous that sometimes merely the smell of them would eat the nose from a man's face. A certain species of woodpecker was the only thing that could destroy them. Their homes were in trees, on which their poisonous tracks could be traced. They often entered the horns of a deer; hence the Indian hunter's first move after shooting a deer was to examine its horns, and if they were infected, the hunter would run away, since he knew that the moment the animal died the fatal insect would emerge from the horn. Around the trees in which they lived deer ever congregated, seemingly bewitched by these fierce and noxious little flies.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

passages.text: Buckskin and deerskin were used to catch them. The bird that killed them for food was colored black and yellow. In the evening it came forth from its home in a hollow tree and scoured the forests for them. These birds were caught with buckskin traps and their feathers were used as charms, being fastened to the arrows of the hunter. An arrow thus made potent would surely bring down the deer.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. III; public domain.

title.en: The Bird of Wampum and the Boy Archer

region.en: The 'tree of promise' between two tribes at war
region.zh: 交戰兩族之間的「應許之樹」

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'Origin of wampum'

summary.en: A man finds in the forest a huge bird coated with clustered wampum; the head chief offers his beautiful daughter to whoever captures it. Each arrow barely draws off some of the coating, which multiplies like the Lernaean hydra's heads. Warriors of the tribe bar a boy of the enemy tribe from shooting; the chief says, 'He is a mere boy; let him shoot on equal terms,' and the boy brings down the bird with unequaled skill. Marrying the chief's daughter, he divides the wampum between the tribes, peace is declared, and he decrees that wampum shall be the price of peace and blood - hence belts of wampum satisfy violated honor.
summary.zh: 有人在林中見一巨鳥，滿身貝珠；大酋長許諾以美麗女兒為賞。眾箭僅能剝落少許，而珠衣如九頭蛇之首，愈剝愈多。敵族前來看熱鬧的男孩被拒射，酋長卻說：「他只是個孩子，讓他與勇士們公平競射。」男孩技驚四座，射落神鳥。他娶酋長之女，將貝珠分贈兩族，締結和平，並立誓貝珠為償血價和平之幣——此後以貝珠帶賠償受辱之名譽。

passages.text: A man while walking in a forest saw an unusually large bird covered with a heavily clustered coating of wampum. He immediately informed his people and chiefs, whereupon the head chief offered as a prize his beautiful daughter to one who would capture the bird, dead or alive, which apparently had come from another world. Whereupon the warriors, with bows and arrows, went to the 'tree of promise,' and as each lucky one barely hit the bird it would throw off a large quantity of the coveted coating, which, like the Lernaean hydra's heads, multiplied by being cropped.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: At last, when the warriors were despairing of success, a little boy from a neighboring tribe came to satisfy his curiosity by seeing the wonderful bird of which he had heard, but as his people were at war with this tribe he was not permitted by the warriors to try his skill at archery, and was even threatened with death. But the head chief said, 'He is a mere boy; let him shoot on equal terms with you who are brave and fearless warriors.' His decision being final, the boy, with unequaled skill, brought the coveted bird to the ground. Having received the daughter of the head chief in marriage, he divided the oh-ko-aeh between his own tribe and that into which he had married, and peace was declared between them. Then the boy husband decreed that wampum should be the price of peace and blood, which was adopted by all nations. Hence arose the custom of giving belts of wampum to satisfy violated honor, hospitality, or national privilege.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.
